2.	Answered by 1.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved concurrence in 'the resolutions adopted in the committee of ways and means respecting the War Revenue Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to move an amendment to the motion, as follows:

Special War Revenue Act
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be struck out and the following added thereto:
the said resolution be resubmitted to the com-mdtee of the whole with instructions to amend the same by striking out section 4 thereof.
Section 4 of the resolution deals with the tax imposed on the transfer of mining and other shares. This tax whs originally enacted in 1920. It was essentially a war measure. As matters now stand, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Roibb) has indicated that he has a very substantial surplus. This tax in its operation is unjust, inequitable and unfair. In addition it is a tax that is essentially imposed upon provincial resources. The Dominion succeeds in obtaining an income tax from provincial companies operating in the development of the resources of the provinces, and this tax imposed upon the transfer of shares is a form of taxation that in my opinion should be left wholly available to the provinces. It should not be a tax resorted to by the Dominion at all. It is double taxation. It imposes a tax on industry; it retards development; it is unjust and inequitable in its operation, as indicated by many hon. members of this house; it is a tax which I think cannot be defended. It is for that reason, sir, that without making any extended address to the house at this time I move this amendment at the first available opportunity, before the resolution is finally adopted by the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is quite right in saying the tax was first introduced under the special War Revenue Act assented1 to on July 1, 1920. It was amended in 1922. It is well that the house and the country should understand at once what my hon. friend is proposing by this amendment. I imagine there has never been a time within recent years when there was so much speculating on the stock exchanges throughout the country as there has been during the past year. I submit there is a general feeling all over the Dominion that the national treasury might very well profit somewhat by this speculation. If a man is disposed to take a gamble on the market and risk his money, is it not reasonable to suppose that he might at least put a little of it in the national treasury to take care of the obligations of the country? My hon. friend now proposes to wipe out this tax entirely because a few people have objected to a certain readjustment of the taxation on the transfer of mining shares. Well, the revenue from this source is only a penny's worth compared with the revenue we get from these special taxes. Although there has been so much speculating on some of the stock
exchanges where they deal largely in these mining shares, the revenue we have been getting from the business is very small, and the revenue we will receive under t'he revised taxation will be comparatively very small.

That is the reason- we
want to wipe it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On transfers of shares and
bonds of every kind, good, bad and indifferent, the total revenue received in 1926-27 was $282,576.50. We improved considerably on that in 1927-28, when we received $615,354. Where did these taxes come from? They did not come from the province of British Columbia, where there is a great mining area, because the records show that in 1926-27 all we received from the Vancouver stock exchange was $1,672.32. In 1927-28 we received from the same source $7,263.44. W'hat did we get from the Toronto Standard mining exchange? In 1926-27 we received $47, 393.01.

But the Toronto mining
exchange deals in British Columbia shares too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possibly. Does that make it any better?

No, but the minister said
he did' not get much from British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, let us add the two together. All we received was $47,393 from the Toronto Standard exchange and $1,672.32 from the Vancouver stock exchange for 1926-27. It is true that in 1927-28 we received $121,114.70 from the Toronto Standard mining exchange and $7,263.44 from the Vancouver stock exchange. But we received from the Montreal stock exchange in 1927-28, $280061.57, and from the Toronto stock exchange, $132,756.60. I am sure my hon. friend has not considered this or he would not move an amendment to strike out this tax in toto, simply because some people who wish to speculate in mining shares abject to the tax.
In the debate the other day the complaint was largely on the ground that what are called "penny" -stocks-the lower priced stocks- would be unfairly discriminated against. Now under this taxation in its amended form if a man wants to take a flyer in the market and buys a thousand shares at 50 cents or less, it will cost him only a dollar. But to save him that dollar my hon. friend proposes to wipe out the tax on a thousand shares at $100 each from which we would receive $40. I submit to my hon. friend that this is not very good economics. No person who wants to speculate in a thousand shares
Special War Revenue Act

at 50 cents or less is injured if he has to pay a tax of one dollar. If he is ready to take a gamble of that kind, surely he should not object to putting a dollar in the national treasury.

Perhaps the minister
does not mind if I ask him a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no.

I suppose he is aware that all the provinces are taxing these transfers of shares. My objection goes essentially to that feature, that it is their business, and as they impose these taxes we should not be duplicating that form of taxation. We did it for the first time right after the war. I say it is a war measure that should now disappear so that we may let the provinces have the field to themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the provinces are only taxing these mining and oil shares.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are right, they do tax the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not all of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provinces of Quebec and Ontario do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think all the
provinces do.
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The time may come when we should have a readjustment between provincial and federal taxation, but meanwhile I ask, is it good judgment on the part of the hon. leader of the opposition, in order to save the purchaser of one thousand 50 cent shares one dollar in taxation, to wipe out a tax that we hope will give us at least as much as it did last year, when we collected $615,000.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the reply of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) meets the case at all. He selects one item and indicates that there is to be a loss of revenue. He has already stated that the revenue at present is not a serious matter, that is, the total for 1927-28 was, I think, $615,000. What is it that the minister proposes to do? I think the house should get this clearly in its mind. He is repealing a stamp tax which was launched during the period immediately following the war when this country was put to extremes in order to get further revenue for unexpected and new expenditures arising out of the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The problem still exists.

Since that time the minister has come to the house year after year boasting of increases in revenues. Here is an item which is producing a revenue of between six and seven hundred thousand dollars. He is promising to wipe that out and substitute for it a very onerous tax

not simply a stamp tax on documents, that is what it amounted to before, but a tax on property, because it is the exchange of property, that he is now taxing. Our contention is that, as applicable to mining, this proposal aims a serious blow at the development of this national, basic, industry. It will affect mining, not because it is a stamp tax but because it is an actual tax upon property, that is the share ownership in mines.
Now, this year the government has refused to assist two very important requirements of the people; one, technical education, and the other, the extension of the good roads system. In connection with the mining industry of Canada, in practically every province, particularly in northern Ontario, northern Quebec, northern Manitoba and British Columbia, the provincial governments are being called upon, I venture to say, to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars for roadways and other facilities in these new mining districts. The government have refused this session to give any assistance to the provinces in the matter of new highways-absolutely refused it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicated that he considered a contribution of that kind to the provinces to be a vicious principle; he will not charge me with misquoting him in attributing that phrase to him. I say, they have absolutely refused to give any assistance in that direction. And now the minister says that he will tax the mining industry and obtain a large revenue therefrom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not the mining industry.

Well, that is where we
differ. The minister is making a distinct change in principle in this tax. He is repealing a section which is essentially a stamp tax. I have already pointed this out, but the minister does not realize the seriousness of it: he is repealing what is essentially a stamp tax, an ordinary stamp upon documents. That is what he has in the existing law, and he is substituting for it a heavy, an onerous tax; it is undoubtedly an onerous tax. My hon. friend from South Timiskaming (Mr. Lang), my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Lawson), my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) and one or two other hon. gentlemen

Special War Revenue Act
have produced figures that are incontrovertible, showing clearly that in many cases the new proposal will render business impossible. I venture to say that the outcome of this will be, if it goes into force even after the amendment the minister introduced the other day, that mining concerns will have to abandon the issue of low priced stocks-that is, stocks at five and ten cents a share, which is the basis on which the mining industry in this country has been built. There is no use in our talking about stopping speculation; this will not seriously affect speculation in stocks in a large way, although it will affect speculation in the cheaper or penny' stocks. In other words, it will largely deprive the mining industry' of Canada of the opportunity to secure capital to carry on its operations.
The other day the minister was impressed, I think, with the arguments, particularly of the hon. members whom I have mentioned, in xhe presentation of the subject; the hon. member for South Timiskaming in particular went into the matter carefully. But the minister is persisting. I have tried to discover a motive and I think I have found it. The minister proposes to impose this onerous tax this year and to put it into force, and he will come to the house next year anid cut the tax down to half or a quarter, or wipe it out, and then tell the people how he is reducing taxation. That is the only excuse for his putting on this tax; there seems to be no other. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) applauds that; he says "That's fine." He endorses it.

Does not my hon. friend
think, as a veteran politician, that that is good politics?

I think it is rotten politics; I think it is disgraceful politics. The minister has done this in regard to the sales tax and lias pot away with it. He raised the sales tax from 3 to 4 and to 6 per cent, and then he lowered it gradually to 2 per cent, and every year he took full credit for the reduction. He intends this year to increase the present tax to a degree which is not warranted and which he knows is not warranted and he will come back next year and cut the tax down and tell the people of the mining districts how he is reducing taxation. He will tell my hon. friend from South Timiskaming, "It is all right; there is no election this year, but next year there is an election and I will cut the tax down."
That is right.

An hon. gentleman says
that is right; I am glad they are endorsing
it. My hon. friend from South Timiskaming spoke most effectively on this question the other day. We had not heard his voice in the house before but we were glad to hear it then. He made an incontrovertible case- what for? For the new mining district of northern Ontario. Now I had a wire-I am sorry it is not here-which reached me the other day from Vancouver, urging me strongly to oppose tliis proposal, not because the people there were opposed to paying a fair tax on the transfer of stocks; not at all. The people there have never squealed at reasonable taxation. But my correspondent points out actual cases on the stock exchange in Vancouver where an individual sells a small block of cheap shares, and under this proposal, after paying the tax, he will have very little left and in fact will incur an actual loss on the transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Right there, will my hon.
friend say that $1 per 1.000 shares is unreasonable?

I say that SI per 1,000
shares at 5 cents a share is too much. One dollar per 1,000 at 50 cents a share is not too bad, but it is the 5 cent shares I am discussing particularly. On this the tax will amount to 2 per cent. Will any hon. gentleman say that is a fair tax on a transaction of that character-a tax of 2 per cent? Will anyone say that is fair in a transaction which is taxed both ways? That sale having gone through, the moment a transfer is made again another tax is levied, and so on. Moreover, there is the provincial tax with commission on top of that. It makes the transaction impossible. And our contention is that the minister has no right to invade that field. The minister asks me whether I think this tax on 1,000 shares at 50 cents is too much. But that is the maximum of that class. Come down to the 5 cent shares and it is shown conclusively that the tax is utterly unreasonable. And some of the best mines in this country-Teck Hughes is one-were financed in their early stages on the 5 cent basis. The minister proposes a tax of 2 per cent on 5 cent shares, but that is not the whole story. Assume that this share is sold three or four times in the year: that means 10 per cent. And so you might go on through the various transactions.
The minister is wrong in his conception of this matter. The tax is exceedingly onerous. The very question which the minister asks me shows that the tax is unfair, because the man who sells shares of the 50 cent class pays exactly the same as t'he man who sells at 5 cents. That is the unfairness of it. One is a $50 transaction and the other a $5 trans-
Special War Revenue Act

action; yet they pay the same tax. If it were fair and equitable the man who sold at 5 cents would not pay the same as the man selling at 50 cents. Take comparisons in a score of different classifications and you find that in every one of these classifications there is a spread which is utterly unfair. I am reminded too of this-it has been pointed out before: 1,000 shares of Noranda at $54 represents $54,000, with a $30 tax. Does not the minister see 'how unfair the tax is?
I come back to the point from which I started:	We are repealing a stamp tax involving a small charge of 3 cents or something like that on the transfer of certain documents. I am not saying that this is entirely equitable, but it is a stamp tax applying to the exchange of documents. But this is a tax on the exchange of property, namely, shares in mines. It might be any other property; it does not matter; we are speaking of mines because that is our chief activity. I submit again that it is utterly unfair; it is a tax that Should not be added to Dominion taxation.
The minister has boasted of his $60,000,000 surplus this year; yet he is now increasing a tax which last produced1 some $600,000, and increasing it to such a degree that it will actually run into millions. There is no doubt that it will run into several millions. That is not the way to impose taxation in a country where the Minister of Finance boasts of his surpluses. If you have a surplus of revenue the proper thing to do is to budget so that your revenue and expenditure shall balance, with a fairly safe margin on the revenue side. That is proper budgeting. But in a country like this it is not the proper thing to budget for huge surpluses. Certainly a surplus is always welcome, but it is not proper to budget for surpluses. That is what the minister is doing, and I think we are warranted in opposing this measure and in asking the support of the house for the deletion of section 4 from the resolution.
Before my hon. friend takes his seat, could he inform the house what taxes are imposed on the sale of shares?

I could not say exactly.
There is a tax on the sale; there is a tax on the purchase by the stockbroker in the stock exchange; there is a provincial tax, which is a perfectly proper tax, on the transfer of shares, and there is this tax which the minister is now seeking to impose.
Is there any tax on shares when they are first, sold?

Under the present law the first issue is not taxed; if the first issue is handed to a broker and distributed by him to other brokers there is no tax, but when the stock leaves the broker and goes to the purchaser there is a tax.

Mr. Speaker, for a few moments I
wish to deal with the figures given the house the other evening by the Minister of Finance, when he was showing how the proposed tax would work out in creating revenue. As an illustration the minister took the figures from one particular day's sales on the Standard stock exchange in Toronto. On that day there were sold 324.900 shares valued at from one cent to fifty cents per share, with an estimated total value of $81,225. Under the present proposal the tax on the sale of those shares would amount to $324.90. Then there were 186,500 shares sold valued at from fifty cents to $1 per share, and under the present proposal the tax collected on that sale would be $466.25. There were sold 114,900 shares over $1 per share and under $3, on which the tax would amount to $1,149; there were 150,900 shares valued at over $3 but not over $20, on which the proposed tax would amount to $3,018, and his last figures were 29,300 shares valued at over $20 and under $100, upon which the proposed tax would amount to $879.
Just for a moment I would like to compare as fairly as I can the tax which it is now proposed to collect on the sale of these shares with the tax which would be collected if we had an ad valorem tax, which is the only fair tax if we must have any at all. On the day taken by the minister 324,900 shares of stock were sold at from one cent to fifty cents per share. I am going to average those shares at twenty-five cents each, and in so doing I am being more than fair to the minister, because if he will look over the records he will find that in the cheaper stocks the majority sell for from ten to twenty cents per share and then the price goes up to over fifty cents. However, we will take the medium price of twenty-five cents per share and see what tax would be collected at the rate of three-twentieths of one per cent, or fifteen cents on each $100 worth of sales. Just here I might explain, how I arrive at the rate of three-twentieths of one per cent. According to the figures given by the minister the total selling price of the shares dealt in that day was $3,886,800, and under the proposed tax the revenue would amount to $5,837.15. If you divide the amount collected into the amount of the sales you get the figure of three-twentieths of

Special War Revenue Act
one per cent on the value or fifteen cents on every $100 worth of shares sold, or in other words just five times the old tax which has been in force ever since 1922. That is, it would be five times the old tax of three cents on every $100 of value if that had been collected as an ad valorem tax on all the sales, but as I showed the other night that was not the case. That tax was only collected on a few of the shares and always on the lower priced stock, so that really for the last seven years the revenue under this tax has been derived mainly from the low priced stocks, and that principle will be continued under the proposed tax, as I intend to show; these low priced stocks will continue to bear the heavy load all the time, instead of that load being equally divided over all issues.
As I have already pointed out, on the 324,900 shares valued at from one cent to fifty cents per share there would1 be collected $324.90, under the present proposal. Taking an average price of twenty-five * cents per share, the sale price of these shares would be $81,225, and a tax of fifteen cents per $100 of valuation would bring in only $121 in revenue. In other words, on this first item under the present proposal the minister would collect two and a half times as much as would be collected under an ad valorem tax. Then his next figures were for stocks valued at fifty cents to one dollar, and 186,500 shares of this stock passed over the exchange on the day he took as an example. At an average price of seventy-five cents a share the total sales price of these shares would be $139,875. Under the proposed tax the revenue from those shares would amount to $466.25, while under an ad valorem tax of fifteen cents per $100 of value he would collect only $210. Then we come to the next class, 114,900 shares valued at from $1 to $3, and at an average price of $2 per share the total selling price of these shares would be $229,800. Under the proposed tax he would collect on the sale of those shares $1,149; with an ad valorem tax of 15 cents per $100, the revenue received would be $345.
The next transaction mentioned by the minister was 150,900 shares at over $3 and under $20 per share. I took an average of $11 per share as being the fair price between those two figures. A sale of 150,900 shares at $11 per share would amount to $1,659,900. Under the proposed tax the revenue would be $3,018 and under an ad valorem tax it would amount to $2,490. In that case an ad valorem tax of 15 cents on $100 would be getting off a little cheaper than under the proposed tax.
The next transaction mentioned was 29,300 shares at over $20 and under $100 per share. I took an average price of $60 per share, which makes the value of the transaction $1,758,000. Under the proposed tax the revenue would be $879 while the ad valorem tax would return a revenue Of $2,637. The revenue is only about one-third of what it would be with the ad valorem tax while on the cheaper shares the present tax will bring in a revenue of between two or four times the amount which would be received with the ad valorem tax. There is not a vestige of fairness in .imposing taxation such as this. I cannot see how anyone would have the effrontery to attempt to justify such an unfair tax. It may be to a lesseir degree, but nevertheless it is continuing along the old line of taxing the smaller man ait a higher rate than the tax imposed upon the big man. There is no justification for it and I cannot understand why the Minister of Finance insists upon trying to impose this tax. I would like t'o quote from the remarks of the Minister of Finance which he made the other evening in an attempt to justify the tax upon the speculative stocks, as he called them. As appears on page 2454 of Hansard, the minister said:
As soon as they begin speculating then certainly th,e nation has a right to take'some share of the profits. If I were representing a mining section of the country I might take a onesided view of the matter. But this is in the interests , of the mining industry, and in support of that statement I shall quote the opinion of the Northern Miner.
I will give that quotation later, but at present I desire to deal with the minister's first statement. I do not agree with the minister because whether you call it speculating or gambling, if there were n,ot people who were optimistic enough to speculate-
Take a chance.

-in an endeavour to bring forth the treasures from the mineral lands of this country, then there would be no mining production or mineral development. This tax is being imposed upon the 'prospectors. They are the first ones to speculate or gamble; they speculate not only with the ferw dollars which they have, but they gamble with their time and with their energy; they risk their health and everything else in an attempt to bring about the mineral development of this Canadian nation. Such a statement as that made by the minister is entirely unfair to the people who are doing the pioneer work for this great industry.
If a tax is to be imposed it should not bear too heavily on those who take the risk of
Special War Revenue Act

the initial speculation, the first gamble, which must precede any real development of our mineral resources.
I will continue with the quotations made by the bon. minister from the Northern Miner. As every hon. member of this house knows, that paper is one of the most reputable mining journals which we have in Canada. The Journal was first published in Cobalt during the early days of mining in that section of the country, and continued to be published there until a few weeks ago when it was moved to Toronto. This quotation which the minister read was apparently from an editorial published during the early part of this year, and is as follows:
While the business of company promotion l>3' brokers has lagged lately, reducing the prospector's claim market, fortunately he has never been in such good position to sell first-class discoveries. Dozens of big mining organizations will listen eagerly to his story if he has a good one to tell, and will send engineers hopping by plane to examine. If his show stands up money is waiting, on the nail. Fasy going, long distance deals are completely out of fashion. The prospeotor can get quick action if he is willing to deal with the big companies.
Competition for good ground is so keen that he is sure of good terms.
Then it goes on:
On the whole, it has probably been a good thing for everybody that the promotional game has been slack. Buyers have had a chance to catch their breath and promoters a chance to realize and act upon the new conditions.
Then it says:
The public was overloaded with half-baked propositions.
I take no exception at all to the minister having quoted that editorial to the house. If you take into consideration the time at which the editorial was written, it is a perfectly fair one and I agree with it in every respect. If I do not miss my guess, that editorial was probably written just soon after one of the worst financial disasters happened in connection with one of the oldest and supposed-to-be one of the best-established brokerage firms in the city of Toronto. I have no doubt in the world that editorial was written after that firm suspended operations. That was the Heron Company which closed its doors some time early this year. If the Minister of Finance was looking for something to justify taxing penny stocks in order to keep poor, innocent individuals from being rooked in that sort of game and losing their money, he picked the wrong editorial to support any argument of that kind, because everyone knows to-day that this firm was dealing in one of the high-priced stocks.

betting that the stock was going to go down instead of up, betting probably illegally by going short on International Nickel, one of the best stocks that we have in the country. It was because of that manipulation that the Heron Company had to cease operations, and this caused one of the worst financial disasters that we have had in Canada and a lessening for the time being in the number of people investing in mining stocks. But in my opinion and, I think, in that of every fair-minded man who gives ithe subject any consideration, that only goes to prove again that mistakes are made in the manipulation of high-priced stocks just as in connection with the cheaper stocks. I will leave that editorial by saying simply that if the Minister of Finance thinks so much of the views of the editor of the Northern Miner, I can put his mind at rest at once as to what the editor of that paper thinks about the present proposed tax. He thinks it is absolutely unfair; that it is not fair to the mining industry and particularly to the ones who do the pioneer work and of necessity have to get their money from the cheaper class of stocks. To tax the low-priced stocks more heavily than the higher-priced stocks is, in the opinion of the editor of the Northern Miner, a mistake, no matter who it is made by. The Minister of Finance also said:
The Monetary Times of January II quotes Mr. Norman Urquhart, president of the Standard stock and mining exchange of Toronto, as follows:
And then he gives the quotation. I did not know at the time, but I understand that Mr. Urquhart was one of the gentlemen who were here representing the brokers from Toronto, asking the Minister of Finance not to impose a tax such as this. I am pointing this out just because the minister quotes Mr. Urquhart, and Mr. Urquhart feels that this is not a fair tax and that, it should not be imposed upon the people notwithstanding the statement he made which the minister quoted. Mr. Urquhart's statement is a perfectly fair one coming as it did and when it did. We have had two or three unpleasant incidents in connection with mining this year, and for the life of me I cannot understand how any person could think they could improve conditions by imposing a tax on the people. Nothing bears out such an idea. An incident that happened just shortly before this statement by Mr. Urquhart, one of the Toronto brokers, was in connection with the Jackson-Manion dealings. This caused a flutter in mining circles and among mining investors in this country. Taxing cheap stocks has nothing

Special War Revenue Act
to do with regulating that sort of thing. We have a Companies Act in, Ontario and I expect there are somewhat in all the other provinces similar acts which are supposed to cope with situations of that character, call them "blue-sky" laws if you will. In connection with the Jackson-Manion affair, the managing director and the mine manager are to-day before the courts on a charge of conspiracy or collusion to defraud the investors in that mine. That is all I want to say about that. But it is absurd for anyone to get up before an intelligent body of people and endeavour to leave the impression that by imposing a heavier tax on the smaller-priced stocks, they are going to do anything to make safer the investment of the people who want to put their money into stocks of that kind in order to help mining development in Canada. 1 do not think that is an unfair statement for me to make.
The minister says further:
Then I have another statement made by one of the most prominent bankers in the city ol Toronto, where I suppose more mining shares are sold than in any other city of Canada.
This statement was made by Mr. Bogert. general manager of the Dominion Bank, .in his annual report.
This is a perfectly fair statement by Mr. Bogert, and I have no fault to find with it. It is an optimistic, not a pessimistic statement. It is just what one would expect from the head of a financial institution of that kind. In the paragraph which the minister quoted there is not- one word to lend any colour for any person to think that good would be done by imposing a heavier tax on the sale of shares, and particularly a heavier tax on the sale of the smaller-priced shares than upon the higher-priced.
Then the minister crosses over to England to tell us that they have a graduated scale of taxation on shares. Everyone must and does know that the people of the motherland are carrying a heavier burden of taxation than probably any other people in the world. They are doing that because of the vast obligations which have been staring them in the face ever since the war. I think it would be entirely unfair for any of us in this house to pass any opinion upon the sort of taxation which the British people in their wisdom have imposed upon themselves, and I say again that their taxation has absolutely no bearing upon the case with which we are dealing at the present time.
Before leaving this tax schedule which I made up from the figures which the Minister of Finance himself gave the other evening, I would like to summarize it. The amount of
the sales for the day he quoted was 13,866,800. On that amount, if this tax goes into effect, he would collect $5,837. I worked out what rate of taxation that would represent, and it works out to 15 cents on each $100 of value sold. The old tax that we have had since 1922 and which will remain in force until it is replaced by this new one, if it goes into effect, amounted to 3 cents on every $100, not of value, but of par value, and as was pointed out so well the other evening that tax was collected on only a very small proportion of the total volume of business done. The tax was falling on the small investor all the time, and if this new tax goes into effect it will still be the small investor who will have bo pay the bulk of the taxation. You would think that after this house had looked into the matter and found out that for the last eight years the small investor is the one who has been most heavily taxed, we would now give him a little advantage to make up for the disadvantage which he has been suffering in the past. But no, a new tax is being brought down under which the small investor is going to continue to be taxed at the expense of the few and bigger investors.
Mr. AD8HEAD:	I understand that the
first sale of shares is not taxed, but only succeeding sales. How can the succeeding sales be of any benefit to the mining company?

I will answer that as best I
can. I do not think that it has yet been made absolutely clear to this house that all of the first issue of stock is entirely free from taxation.
How can succeeding sales benefit the company?

Very often when a new company is formed, some one undertakes the underwriting of a certain amount of the treasury stock. For example, I cited a case the other night of a company selling one million shares at 5 cents a share in order to raise $50,000. On the sale of that stock they would be taxed $1,000 under this proposed tax.
Not on the first transfer.

All right. Whoever underwrites the stock guarantees to the treasury of the company 5 cents a share for that one million shares, in order to raise $50,000 for the company. Then the underwriter sells the stock to the public, and that stock is taxed. That is the way it works out.
Since this proposal was brought down by the Minister of Finance, I have received a letter from British Columbia-I am not
Special War Revenue Act

familiar with conditions there, but the British Columbia members will know whether this is correct or not-stating that in British Columbia, where the mining industry has been undergoing great development in the last year, they raise the money for the initial development pretty nearly all through selling these cheap priced shares to the public, and to a far greater extent than we do in Ontario. .
Absolutely correct.

That is the information I have. The mining industry in Ontario is older, and we have mining people who have money and have been interested in mining for years who will speculate or gamble on the further development of the minerals of our province, and we do not so often go to the public with cheap priced stocks to raise the initial development money. Probably a syndicate of five or ten men will put up $50,000 or $100,000, after they have had their engineers look over the property and they are satisfied that the geological conditions are such that the property has a chance and may develop into a mine. It is always a gamble in the first instance. I do not care how good a prospect may iook, it is nothing but a gamble, and anyone who has had anything to do with mining knows that. But what is the use of saying, just because it is a gamble and people might lose their money, the government might as well take some of that money because the stockholders might lose it anyway. Is not that an awful argument to put up?

I did not put it that way. If my hon. friend will permit me,'I bought some oil stock in the Macleod Oil Company some years ago at $1 per share, and the company got 75 cents out of every dollar received from the sale of the shares. They developed a well, and later on I sold the stock for $10 a share. I got $10, but what I want to know is how that benefited the company.

One would need to know all the details of the deal before expressing an opinion. The hon. member benefited all right, and that is the main thing. He gambled and in that case won. In a lot of other cases he might not be so lucky.
Under those circumstances what Objection would there be to the hon. member for East Calgary paying a tax to the government?

If he wants to pay a tax
I do not object, but I say that as long as you tax the cheaper priced stocks more heavily than the higher priced stocks you are

doing something that is absolutely unfair and something that cannot possibly be justified. I said when I was speaking on this matter the other evening that I was not a bit afraid of the minister putting on too high a tax if he made it an ad valorem tax. Let it rest fairly and evenly on all the people who are paying the tax. Let it be a tax on the value of the transaction. That is all I have been asking for. That is why I ventured to work out what this rate of taxation would be over the day's business. It would be just five times what it was before. I do not know what the minister is budgeting for in this tax, I do not know how much money he expects to get from it; he has not told us; but I do feel sure that any person who considers conditions in this country to-day will agree with me that there is not a doubt in the world that an immense volume of business will be traded in this year, so that one can hardly estimate it. Last year on the Toronto stock exchange there was a turnover of $600,000,000 dollars. That is only one of the exchanges. There are also the Montreal, the Calgary, the Winnipeg, the Vancouver and the other stock exchanges throughout the country. Undoubtedly vast developments are going on. There is no doubt there will be ten times that value traded in, and a tax of 15 cents on the $100, an ad valorem rate, would bring into the treasury millions of dollars this year.

As I have shown, the Minister of Finance proposes to collect $50 on a sale of $5,000, and I once more assert that no member of this house, no Canadian, is going to participate in financing of that character. Fifty dollars is too high a tax to pay on one transaction. That means that these shares will not be marketable. Let me tell you what is going to happen. Take the Reeves McDonald property, which lies in West Kootenay. It is on the boundary line, practically adjoining Pend d'Oreille, which is in the United States, but it is financed in Canada. Now if this tax had been in force when these two properties were promoted, where does the minister think the promotion would have taken place? Unquestionably it would have been in Spokane, in the United1 States; after all that is the nearest city to these properties and that is where the promotion would have taken place. That is also where future promotions in British Columbia will take place, because the public will not tolerate a tax of $50 where the sale price is only $5,000. The shares will become unmarketable and no man will purchase stock from the underwriters, no matter how promising the properties may be, if he knows that when he sells his stock he will have to pay a tax of $50. These shares turn over ten or twenty times a year, and at the end of the year that $5,000 might pay a tax of $500 or even $1,000.
I am confirmed in my statement with regard to the financing of these properties by the

oldest and most experienced men in the industry in British Columbia. I have received from them telegrams and letters, and they all assert that there can be no question that so far as new promotions and new developments are concerned they must necessarily take place in the United States because our people will not subscribe to them if they are to be taxed in this way. As I have said repeatedly on the floor of this house, in British Columbia since the war we have financed our mining development from our own savings, and the present enactment will create a handicap which will prohibit any future development of that kind. That will leave only one place where in future these promotions may be undertaken; that is the United States, in either Spokane or Seattle.
In addition to that, the trading which is now going on in the Vancouver stock exchange will be transferred to the United States, because you will find that a number of these companies with shares of low market value will perhaps wind up their affairs and reincorporate in the United States. They will list their stocks in that country and they will be traded in no longer on our exchanges. In that case the minister cannot hope to collect the tax which he proposes to impose on these lower priced shares. However, I am speaking for the industry rather than for the companies already in existence; I am looking to future developments. I want future development to take place here in

Special War Revenue Act
Canada and to be financed in Canada; I want the Canadian people to benefit by the development, and I say they cannot do so if the Minister of Finance insists on passing through the house the measure now under consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the unfairness and iniquity of this tax as far as the mining industry is concerned has been abundantly established by the data and the arguments submitted by lion members on both sides of the house. I rise for only a moment in order to place on record a telegram which has been just received by the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. EsLing) from Mr. S. W. Miller, head of the large brokerage firm of Miller and Court Company, Limited, Vancouver. This organization has been instrumental in successfully establishing some of the most important mining enterprises in British Columbia; it is not only a concern interested in the promotion of these enterprises but it is very much concerned in developing the industry. After expressing his appreciation of certain arguments advanced by the hon. member for West Kootenay, Mr. Miller says:
For last fifteen years we have used our time and money to promote development of British Columbia mining, and should the government's present tax pass it is our intention to withdraw absolutely from the mining promotion business. You can appreciate what reaction a move of this kind would have on the mining development of our province.
Apart from the rights of the provinces with respect to taxation of mining enterprises, apart from the question of the division of the field of taxation, in the face of the data which has been submitted and in view of the incontrovertible facts and the judgment of men who understand the business, in this case I think the minister, with that breadth of judgment which he ought to display, should depart from the attitude of obstinacy which the people of Canada will believe to be actuating him if he persists in his present course and reconsider the proposal now before the house. If necessary he might delay proceedings at this time in order to study the facts and obtain full knowledge of the situation so that the best efforts of the government may be devoted to the mining industry of Canada.

it will be seen that a 3 cent stamp is required on the stock certificate, whether it be of a par value of $100 or less, which means a tax of 3 per cent on the par value. As I understand the present amendment, it is proposed to bring it back-
That is 3 cents on

I was endeavouring to
prepare my hon. friends for the shock when I told them that I thought they would disagree with my statement. Upon reading that section I think there is fair ground for saying that this is a specific tax and not an ad valorem tax. It is a specific tax of 3 cents per share for every share of a par value of $100 or fraction thereof.

It is not 3 per cent; it

It is one-third of one
per cent, and I thank my hon. friend for the correction. If the amendment should pass it would bring this tax back to that situation.
The thing which is complained of is the taxation on the so-called penny shares, or the small priced shares. The minister first proposed that he would tax all shares selling at $3 or under at the rate of one cent per share; this would include a $3 share and go right down to the one-sixteenth of a cent per share mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark). It was pointed out that that one cent per share tax would be a pretty heavy tax on the small priced shares, but the minister now proposes that instead of that tax he will impose a one cent tax on shares selling at over $1 and up to $3. That means that there will be a tax of from one per cent to one-third of one per cent on those shares. As to the shares selling below one dollar, the minister now proposes that instead of imposing a one cent per share tax he will impose a tax of a quarter-eent per share on shares selling at not more than a dollar but over 50 cents. That means that the maximum tax would be one-half of one per cent and the minimum tax would be one-quarter of one per cent. Surely

that is not something which would ruin the mining industry, as my hon. friends suggest. Then the minister proposes to impose a tax of one-tenth of a cent per share on shares selling at 50 cents or less. I do not think that that can be regarded as a very heavy tax, because it is less than the tax imposed at the present time. The rate on a 50 cent share would be one-fifth of one per cent and as the price of the share decreases the proportion goes up and the percentage of taxation is a little larger. When you get down to shares selling for one-sixteenth of a cent per share it means a pretty stiff tax, but I do not believe that there are many sound mining companies in this country whose shares are selling on the market at anything like one-sixteenth of a cent per share. Such companies are the ones who have sold their shares and put in their development, and the development has resulted unsuccessfully. The people who invested at that time have found themselves with shares on their hands and I do not think it would make very much difference to them whether their shares sold for one-sixteenth of a cent per share or one-sixtieth of a cent per share. The only thing they can do is to hold on to their shares with the hope of improvement in the situation, and I do not think the house would be very much concerned with that special situation.

Instead of issuing perhaps 5,000,000 shares for a property valued at only $50,000, the number of shares should be reduced and their value increased. The difficulty in the past has been that some mining companies issued' their shares in millions and sold them at between 5 and 10 cents to people, if I may say so, who had no business to buy them but who were attracted by the large number of noughts on the face of the stock certificate and the very small amount of money they had to part with to purchase that imposing looking certificate. With all due respect to those who are interested in the mining industry, I do not believe that the people who are most interested in the mining industry are keen on seeing big lithographed stock certificates put out bearing amounts of hundreds or thousands of dollars on the face of them and selling, let us say, at 50 cents or a dollar or $2 per share. I suggest that it is much better to have the issue so limited that the certificate will sell at a price which will permit of a fair taxation of one-fifth of one per cent, or something of that kind, and regulate the number of shares to be issued by the amount of money which is required.
That is my answer to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard with reference to refinancing. If a company has millions of dollars par value of stock in its treasury at a dollar per share, then they had better pass special resolutions and take the necessary procedure to increase the par value and decrease the number of shares so that they will sell at 50 cents or $1 at least in order that the tax rate may be small, instead of leaving the par value at $1 and selling the shares at one or two cents.

Oh, yes, they do. My intention in rising was to reply to the Minister of National Defence. While he to a certain extent ridicules the old tax, it was much more equitable than the new one. them to-day, but one that I pointed out was a $30 tax on $54,000 worth of Noranda, and a $10 tax on $1,020 worth of Kirkland Lake, the number of shares in each case being the same. We have had several nuisance taxes in this country. The house in committee on Bill No. 25, to amend the Fish Inspection Act-Hon. Mr. Cardin-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section-Extension of application of act.

This bill provides for an
amendment to the Fish Inspection Act in order to include fish-curing establishments, as was recommended by the Atlantic fisheries commission. The bill has been before the standing committee on marine and fisheries, which has approved it. Section 2 deals with the publication of the regulations in the prefix to the annual statutes. The Department of Justice has represented to us that the printing of these regulations in the statutes delays the publication of the statutes. In view of the fact that these regulations are printed in the Canada Gazette it has been decided not to have them published in the statutes.

I do not desire to make any comments with reference to this particular bill, but I should like to take this opportunity of referring to a kindred bill, No. 26, which was before the committee a couple of times. There does not seem to be any disposition on the part of the officials of the department to have the provisions of that bill become effective. Could the minister give us some information in that regard?

The hon. member is certainly mistaken as to the intention of the department. The government is absolutely serious in the bill which has been presented to the house and which is now before the standing committee on marine and fisheries.
Apparently it is going to die there.

I understand that the committee has appointed a subcommittee to look into the evidence and recommendations of the Atlantic fisheries commission with a view to making a report to the whole committee. There has been no undue delay in the consideration of that bill as far as the government is concerned, and I can assure the hon. member that we are desirous of having that bill before the house as soon as possible, and before the session closes.

That bill referred to the
trawler question, and a subcommittee was appointed to look into the evidence taken before the royal commission. The minister must realize that to do this will require a period of some months-because the evidence was very voluminous, consisting of thousands and thousands of pages-and will make it impossible to present the bill to parliament during the present session.

I am sure that the subcommittee will not undertake to read every word in the evidence. They are familiar with the conditions and it will not be necessary for them to read the whole evidence in order to make a report.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

to give a short statement of the expenditures that the harbour commission propose to make out of this appropriation of 810,000,000, if it is granted. The first item is 82,000,000, for the construction of three new berths for the unloading of grain and general cargoes in the harbour. Prior to the present the Tarte wharf was used for the unloading of tramp steamers, but since the development of the grain trade in the port of Montreal and the increase in the storage capacity of elevator No. 3, it has been found impossible to use the Tarte wharf for the purpose for which it was previously employed. It is proposed now to build three new berths at the Laurier wharf, and these three berths will be used in connection with the extended facilities at elevator No. 3. It is expected that the three new berths on this wharf will bring a return of about 880,000 and that on account of the increase in the grain traffic in that section of the harbour there will be an increase in revenue of about 850,000, so that the engineers and technical experts of the commission estimate that the return on this expenditure of 82,000,000 will be 8130,000.
The second item provides for an expenditure of 82,000,000 for the reconstruction of two old wharves, King Edward and Alexandra, in the centre of the harbour. These wharves are used at present by the bigger vessels of 16,000 to 20,000 tons coming into the harbour of Montreal. These wharves were built thirty years ago, and the engineers of the harbour commission have been for several years representing to the commission that it is absolutely necessary to rebuild these old wooden structures.
Item No. 3 provides for an expenditure of
81,500,000	for the extension of the electrical system beyond the canal. The property of the harbour commission is divided by the Lachine canal and the electrical system of the section of the harbour east of the canal is operated by the Canadian National while the other, or main section of the harbour is operated by the electrical system of the harbour commission. Last year the harbour commission handled 150,000 revenue cars in the main section of the harbour and in the section of the harbour beyond the Lachine canal 50,000 revenue cars were handled by the Canadian National. It is a source of great inconvenience to have one section served by the electrical system of the harbour commission and the other by the Canadian National. The idea is to extend the electrical service of the main section of the harbour to the eastern section beyond the canal.

Therefore the advice of the expert confirms the belief of the commissioners that the harbour of Chicoutimi is by far the more advantageous of the two. Of course I understand there is a certain amount of dispute between the two localities, but from an engineering point of view there is no doubt that Chicoutimi is by far the better place,, and it is also much nearer the centre of the industrial development which is taking place in that section.

The minister informed the committee that he expected a revenue of $160,000 per annum. He also gave the various items that go to make up the total. Can he inform us when he expects to reach that amount of revenue?

As soon as the facilities
are provided, as soon as the wharves are built, the traffic will commence there because the industries are waiting for the development of these facilities to handle the larger amount of supplies they propose to handle.

Chicoutimi Harbour Commission

Do I understand that
these industries cannot develop until such time as the facilities are provided, or what are they doing with the business now?

They are handling the
business as well as they can, but they are not at the present time importing into Chicoutimi the same amount of supplies that they will be in a position to import when the industries are completely established. These mills are in the course of completion, and the harbour commissioners want to be ready, when the mills are in operation, with the necessary facilities in the harbour.
I take it that the total expenditure, after this item is passed, will be $2,500,000?
Yes.

Has the government
lent any money to the Ha-Ha harbour the minister was talking about?
No.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 69, to provide for a further loan to the Halifax harbour commissioners.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 2-Loan of $5,000,000 to corporation for construction of terminal facilities.

In regard to this bill I am iiot in a position to give any extensive or detailed statements as far as the past year is concerned, because the harbour commissioners were put in possession of the facilities of the harbour only during the latter months of last year. An advance of $500,000 was authorized a few years ago for the harbour of Halifax, out of which there has so far been expended $31,095.65. The elevator up to recently was under the control of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the information we have from that department as to the grain shipped through it is as follows:

A summary of the proposed expenditure which has been submitted to me is as follows :
