Was there any revenue
last year?
I have no statement as to that, but the revenue would amount to practically nothing, because, as I have said, the commissioners took over the property late last year.
The revenue from the elevator would come under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Yes.

From the statement of the minister it appears that 1,000,000 bushel additional capacity is to be provided at a cost of $300,000. Does the commission feel that this will be justified? What is the present elevator capacity?

Speaking from memory,
2,000,000 bushels.

And you have just filled that elevator once, because the number of bushels passing through last year was 2,000,000. I would recommend that the minister look into that question, because an elevator can handle a great deal more grain in the year than its capacity, and additional capacity should not be built until there is greater volume. A few days ago I inquired whether the elevator had been leased. The minister's information was that he did not think so. Can the minister say now whether any bin room in that elevator has been leased to private parties?

We have nothing to indicate that the elevator has been leased to anyone.

Halifax Harbour Commission
Did the minister have the files of the Trade and Commerce department examined to see whether a previous lease had been given by that department?

No. All the information we have in my department indicates that the elevator is still under the control of the hiarbour commission. The commissioners, having taken possession of the property only last year, would certainly have advised the department if the elevator had been leased. Such a thing would not have been done without the consent and approval of the department.

I have received information that the bin room in the elevator had been leased to private parties for the purpose of mixing Canadian and American grain. If that is the case, naturally we would take very strong objection to it. May I suggest that the minister make further inquiries to see whether that is being done?
Certainly.
I have received representations from my constituency concerning top wharfage at Halifax. This is being charged as a result of the establishment of the harbour commission.
We told you that last year.

I would like to place a few facts before the minister for his consideration. The Halifax harbour commission was established, as hon. gentlemen know, as a result of one of the recommendations of the Duncan commission. Prior to the establishment of the commission the wharves at Halifax were owned by the Canadian National Railways. The item of freight in which I am particularly interested is apples coming from the Annapolis valley. Several million dollars worth of apples go through the port of Halifax every year. The charge for top wharfage on apples prior to the establishment of the commission was 4 cents a barrel. The harbour commission has established a rate of 1 cent a barrel, *which so far as I can learn is probably the most moderate rate in Canada. But the shippers of the Annapolis valley were not called on to pay top wharfage charges. The (Canadian National Railways shared in the transportation of the apples to a slight extent and they charged what they called a switching charge, part of which the shippers paid. The shippers still have to pay their proportion of the switching charge; but the wharves having been taken over by the Halifax harbour commission, a top wharfage charge is now imposed by the commission, which is just that much of an addition to
what the shippers all along the Dominion Atlantic Railway have to pay. The charge, as I say, is moderate, and as the whole of Nova Scotia, I think I am safe in saying, was in favour of the establishment of the Halifax harbour commission-certainly I received many resolutions from boards of trade, asking that I support the establishment of the commission-I do not think any very reasonable exception can be taken to the charge. But it is thought that to the extent that it is imposed upon freight coming from points along the Canadian National Railways it should be absorbed by that system. If that situation arises-absorption of the top wharfage rate by the Canadian National Railways, which is quite proper-there should be a similar absorption by the other transportation system, or at least some arrangement should be made so there would be no discrimination between the shippers on the Canadian National system and the shippers on the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which is part of the Canadian Pacific Railway system. I bring these facts to the attention of the minister for his consideration. The matter is of some importance because the shippers of the Annapolis valley send a great deal of freight to foreign countries through the port of Halifax.

The minister mentioned an
expenditure of $100,000 for land damages. Has he any particulars as to whom those damages were paid?
I regret that I have not the details before me, but I will undertake to supply them to my hon. friend.

I should like to bring to
the attention of the minister the same matter that my friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) has referred to. Prior to the establishment of the commission I understand there was no top wharfage charge, that it was absorbed either by the railways or by the steamship companies. The constituency which I have the honour to represent in that district ships upwards of 1,000,000 barrels of apples annually. Naturally the shippers protest most vigourously against this Charge. I trust the minister will take the matter into consideration and see if some arrangement cannot be made whereby either the railway companies or the steamship companies will absorb this charge. It means quite a tax on the shippers. We were all in favour of the establishment of the harbour commission, but we were led to believe there would be no ad-

Halifax Harbour Commission
vance whatever in the charges. I am glad my hon. friend from Hants-Kings has brought the matter up, and certainly it should receive consideration by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I feel sure the harbour commissioners will be most anxious to make the port of Halifax as popular as possible with shippers. They know the conditions of the province and I am confident they will do their utmost to meet any representation made to them by the shippers of Nova Scotia. If they are in need of any advice along the lines suggested by my hon. friends, I shall be quite willing to tender it.

So far as I know,
every public harbour which comes under the direction of harbour commissioners finances itself by certain charges imposed on all shippers. While I deeply sympathize with the shippers through the port of Halifax, I certainly see no reason to suppose that they should be treated in any way different from the shippers through other ports. I have always understood that the money we lend is to be expended by the harbour commissioners to provide improvements for facilitating the shipment of goods, and therefore it is to be expected that the shippers will have to meet a part of that cost. I should like to know whether the suggestion made by the two hon. members from the Annapolis valley is to be treated as an exception to the general rule.

I think the tariff of rates
that the hon. gentlemen have been complaining of is prevailing generally in all the other harbours.
That is my impression.

Although it is desirable that the charges be the same in all harbours, there is always room for certain exceptions according to the locality in which the port is situated. We have to take care of the special conditiotas surrounding a particular line of trade. But certainly it is expected the harbour commissioners will make their charges high enough to pay the interest on the money we are advancing to them. However, we always try to have the charges as low as possible.

I am quite in agreement with the minister that the charges to cover the cost involved should be as low as possible. It has always been my impression that however those charges are absorbed, in the long run the shippers and the consumers of the goods on which such charges are levied
[Mr. Short.!
must meet them. If they are absorbed by the transportation companies, they will certainly be included in the freight rates, and eventually they will be reflected back in the prices which the shippers will receive for their goods.	[DOT]
My main point is that the Shippers on the two transportation systems should be treated in the same way; there should be no difference.
Certainly.

I ventured last year to
express the opinion that Halifax and St. John should be free ports, and it was suggested during the course of the debate that the words 'Tree port" had been misunderstood by myself. If the minister has been following the observations of the trade commissioner at Hamburg, who recently has been making addresses throughout Canada, he will realize that this gentleman has advocated exactly what I then suggested to the house. I suggested that in our export business we were competing with the world by reason of the fact that the home market was by this government handed over to our foreign competitors, necessitating our seeking foreign markets for exports for which we should be able to find markets at home; and as we were driven to foreign markets we have to compete not only with the domestic markets in those foreign countries but, as well, with other competitors throughout the world. This being so, the question of charges-top wharfage and charges of that character in connection with export trade-becomes very important. This gentleman from Hamburg in, I believe, his address at Prince Rupert, pointed out the inevitable result and he further indicated the experience in Hamburg, where he is stationed, giving particulars of the whole matter. I shall not go into this to-night beyond observing that the recommendation of the Duncan report was that these harbours should be put under a commission. I had no doubt when I read that report, nor have I any doubt now about this:	It was not intended that these ports
should be regarded as commission ports in the sense in which we ordinarily use that term, implying self-sustaining undertakings, but that they should be considered' to be national ports out of which, summer and winter, goods might be exported in order that the idea which was behind the confederation of the maritime provinces and the other parts of the Dominion should be carried out. That idea was that the export traffic of the country shodld find its way to the ports of the world through Halifax and St. John, during the winter at any

Halifax Harbour Commission
rato, although during the summer, as it was then pointed out, the harbours of Montreal and Quebec afford many facilities in that direction. The conditions to which the hon. member for Hants-Ivings (Mr. Ilsley) has alluded indicate clearly that what I anticipated has happened, namely, that the charges imposed for top wharfage have affected the movement of commodities, such as apples in the Annapolis valley, and commodities of that kind. Whether the traffic originates on the Canadian National Railways or on the Dominion Atlantic, or whether it originates at the port of St. John, the situation is one which, if it continues, cannot but be injurious to the ports and must bring about a condition which will prevent the accomplishment of the purpose intended in the expenditure of the monies in question; because these expenditures are made for these ports as national undertakings; they are ports through which it is intended that Canadian goods shall be shipped to the markets of the world. That is the position as I understand it, and I think the minister must approach the question in the light of the Duncan report from a different angle than he otherwise would. These are not ports of the character of those that are closed during a portion of the year.

Section agreed to.
Sections 3 to 6 inclusive agreed to.
Title agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the bill?

Before you do so, Mr. Chairman, may I point out that in the last seventy-five minutes we have voted money at the rate of a- quarter of a million dollars per minute. Bill No. 66 provides for a loan to the harbour commission of Vancouver of $10,000,000; Bill No. 67 provides for a loan of $2,000,000 to the harbour commission of Three Rivers; Bill No. 68 provides for a loan of $2,000,000 in connection with Chicoutimi; and this bill, No. 69, makes provision for a loan to the Halifax commission of $5,000,000. This represents a total of $19,000,000. In 1914 plans were drafted for a breakwater at the town of Leamington in the riding of South Essex, which I have the honour to represent, and that proposal involved an expenditure Of $300,000. But although continued representations have been made to this government no favourable consideration has ever been given to the harbour there. I wish to direct this to the attention of the minister so that possibly, in preparing his estimates next year, he may favourably consider a constituency whose colour has not been at all times Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about Halifax?

South Essex used to be Liberal. I may say that I have written to the deputy minister asking that minor repairs be also made to the wharf at Amherstburg and I trust that favourable consideration will be given this matter.

That is something that
comes under the Public Works department, but I will undertake to bring the representations of my hon. friend to the knowledge of my colleague.

I wish to refer briefly to the harbours of Halifax and St. John, and particularly Halifax, in relation to the report of the Duncan commission in its recommendations respecting these harbours. The report recommends that these ports be developed just as the railways and the canals in Canada were developed. Now we all know how the railways of Canada were developed! and particularly how the canal system of this country was developed and is maintained. These undertakings -were carried out at the cost of the Dominion as a whole and are to-day operated without any tolls whatever. Not only does that apply to our own traffic; it applies also to the traffic of our neighbours to the south of us. Now we in Nova Scotia are in this position.: this country is giving to the people to the south of us facilities which enable them to bring in their coal and steel, using for their transport our canals free of all toll charges, to compete with the maritime provinces in Montreal and other cities of central Canada. To balance to some extent the disabilities under which we were labouring in this connection and in some other respects, the Duncan commission made this recommendation with reference to the maritime ports. It is no answer to the recommendations of that commission to say that the government have appointed a commission to regulate, to govern and to operate these harbours when they make no provision for so doing except through tolls levied on the traffic of these harbours. And that is exactly what has happened under the harbour commissions of St. John and Halifax. This was not what was intended or recommended by the Duncan commission, to whose report I have referred. So long as the present condition of affairs prevails we in the maritime provinces will continue to protest against a situation which is very far from that recommended by the Duncan commission. I wish again to call the attention of the minister and of the committee to these facts.

Halifax Harbour Commission

I want to say just a word in regard to this matter. My hon. friend and I do not agree, but since he feels it necessary to put his views on record, I feel that I should not allow the opportunity to pass without oiiee more reminding this committee of the exact situation.
My hon. friend has referred to-night, as he did previously, to the terms of what is now known as the Duncan report. I only desire to direct the attention of the committee to the passages in that report which already have been referred to and which I say with all due respect do not bear out the contention of my hon. friend. The report states clearly that the recommendation is that there shall be statutory commissions appointed. As I had occasion to point out previously the gentlemen who made that report were not unskilled in the use of the English language; they were men with full ability to make their meaning plain, and from cover to cover of the report there is no suggestion that the statutory commissions which were recommended should be different in any degree from the statutory commissions already established at Vancouver, Quebec, Montreal and other places. So clear is this that in the report itself, following the recommendation, Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and his associates expressly refer to the fact that they had an opportunity for a private session with the Montreal harbour commission, and they go on to say:
...and, by hearing from them the steps they took to survey and stimulate production in their immediate territory as well as wider afield, we are confirmed in our view as to what harbour commissions (constituted of business and experienced persons) at Halifax and St. John could .do in stimulating the trade of the maritime provinces.
Then they go on to reiterate their recommendation. Quite contrary to what my hon. friend has said, I am of the opinion that the suggested commissions were similar to those of which Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and his colleagues were fully aware, and if anything more were needed to substantiate that belief I find it in the case which was made before the Duncan commission, during which the gentleman who spoke for the city of Halifax advocated commissions similar to those already established in Montreal and Quebec. Let me just read a portion of the representations which were made. This gentleman said:
Probably the quickest way to bring this to the attention of the commission would be to glance through the annual reports of the harbour commissions of Quebec, Montreal and Vancouver, and you will find in reading their reports that the minds of the commissioners are 
centred principally on the two things: 4Port development and solicitation of traffic;* and inevitably they make a great deal of the improvement in the quantity of traffic moving through the port each year.
There was not a suggestion that fair tolls should not be charged in connection with the business but rather it was thought that the work of these commissions should be principally in improving business and soliciting traffic. Further, this gentleman said:
We have no objection to their solicitation of traffic, and believe that they are acting wisely as trustees for that property, which belongs to the Dominion government; but we do claim, as I stated before, that a similar body should be constituted for the port of Halifax and not with any idea of taking traffic away from Montreal or any other port, but rather in the hope that it will at least offset the competition of these other ports which are being developed by the aid of government money.
I do not think there can be any question but that the ports were to be on the same basis, and tihe aid of government money means just exactly what we are doing tonight, namely the voting of a substantial loan to the harbour commission for the purpose of developing and improving the facilities of that port. No one has suggested that tolls are to be charged which will retard the development and use of these ports. Rather the reverse is the case; after all the Dominion government is advancing this money in order that these facilities may be improved and traffic developed, and tolls are to be charged as they are charged on the railways, namely the rates to be according to what the traffic will bear-

"A Daniel come to
judgment."

I do not know what that means; that is not my name. Perhaps the hon. gentleman refers to my hon. friend who preceded me. I only desire to point out that my hon. friend from Pictou referred to the railways and canals, and said Sir Andrew Rae Duncan also referred to them. He dealt with the canals; let me deal with the railways. The railways were developed through the advancing of large sums of money by the Dominion, but no one has suggested that the railways should not charge tolls. Money is being advanced in the same way to this harbour commission, and I think tolls are properly collected so long as they are not in excess of what the traffic will bear.
That brings me to the question of the free port, brought up by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I do not think he intended to suggest that there should be no tolls paid

Administration in Yukon
at all. Reference was made last year to the free port of Hamburg. It was pointed out that there is a certain area in which goods are not required to pay duty, but Hamburg charges tolls far in excess of those charged at the Atlantic ports of Halifax and St. John.
No.
I dealt with that question last year, and I shall not delay the matter by going over it again to-night.

I have been there, and
I am thoroughly well aware of the conditions prevailing in the free port zone.

I think my hon. friend
from Pictou will agree that considerable advances have been made with respect to Halifax harbour even in the short time it has been under the administration of the harbour commission. There has been a concentration of effort in connection with the solicitation of traffic, in connection with the arrangements whereby certain large steamship companies are calling and in some cases turning there, in connection with a very substantial increase in the general cargo passing through that port, the figures for which I will not trouble the committee with to-night, and in connection with the movement of grain. All these things have come to pass within the last two yeans; I believe the harbour commission are entitled to a great deal of credit and I believe if this committee passes this loan the resulting substantial improvement in facilities will bring about a large increase in the production of traffic and will assist the development of the port as Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and his associates had in mind when they made the report to which my hon. friend has referred.

I am absolutely convinced-and I think I could prove to any unprejudiced group of people-that Sir Andrew Rae Duncan meant one thing, viz:	that
a harbour commission should be brought into being which, as he said, would develop the port. What did that mean? It meant the provision of adequate" facilities for port development, and who was to pay for those facilities? They were to be paid for by the Dominion of Canada, just as the Dominion as a whole paid for the construction of our canal system, and these two maritime ports were to be operated as our canal system is operated, free of tolls or harbour dues. As a matter of fact Halifax was formerly practically free of all tolls on its public wharves, and its harbour facilities were maintained at the expense of the Dominion
before the creation of this commission, but now, in order to meet the interest on the bonds issued by the commission, of necessity tolls must be and are applied, so to-day Halifax has to submit to a system of tolls which it did not have previously.

If my hon. friend will
permit me-

Not now; I did not
interrupt the minister, but he is the champion interrupter of this house; that is his reputation, and it is not creditable to him.
I repeat, that is the situation, and my point is, always has been and will continue to be that what Sir Andrew Rae Duncan meant was that a commission should be appointed to administer this port. The minister refers to the fact that the Duncan commission interviewed- the Montreal harbour commissioners. Of course they did; they did so in order to see how they had developed the harbour of Montreal, not in order to recommend a similar taxing commission for Halifax. In the mind of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan these were to be different commissions altogether; there is no doubt about that. The minister may argue as long as he pleases, but he cannot convince the people of Halifax, the people of Nova Scotia or the people of St. John, New Brunswick, that we have the type of harbour commission which was foreshadowed and intended by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan. That is my answer to the minister.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY

speechtext: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 131, respecting the administration of justice in the Yukon territory.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext:
The
explanatory note in connection with this bill says that because of the geographical location of the northern part of the Yukon territory it may be more convenient to carry on the trials of persons charged with indictable offences committed therein before a magistrate of the Northwest territories. The explanatory note refers to the northern part of the territory but the bill does not, and I would regret to see that principle applied to the whole of the Yukon territory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext:
That is not the intention.
256S
Administration in Yukon

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: That might not be the case with the present Minister of Justice, but I intend to suggest when the bill goes into committee that it be confined to the northern part of the territory. The administration of justice in the Yukon is swift enough, but it is not carried on as it is in the Northwest territories. Not so long ago we had an account of a trial of a criminal case in the northern part of the Northwest territories. A judge was sent up to try a murder charge and the Department of Justice took the precaution of sending a gallows with him. That may have been a very wise precaution but we do not move quite so swiftly in the Yukon.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: What about the hangman?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: I think they found a hangman up there. For these reasons I would like to have the operation of this bill confined to the northern part of the Yukon around the Arctic ocean, and not have it apply to that part of the country where the white people live.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) suggests that the words "alleged to have been committed north of the sixty-fifth parallel of latitude" be added after the word "offence" in the seventh line. Would the hon. member tell me if that would include Herschel island?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: That would include Herschel island and Fort McPherson.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext: Herschel island is away north of that.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY

If you adopt that recommendation you would be excluding from the operation of the bill all that part of the Yukon which is inhabited by white people and where business is being carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE IN THE YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Justice suggests that the following words be added to the section, "and thereupon the court or judge so named shall have jurisdiction to try such person." The section as amended would read:
1. Whenever it appears to the satisfaction of the Minister of Justice that it is expedient to the ends of justice that the trial of any person heretofore or hereafter charged with an indictable offence alleged to have been committed north of the sixty-fifth parallel of latitude in the Yukon territory should be held in some district or place other than that in which the offence is alleged to have been committed or would otherwise be triable, the Minister of Justice may order that the trial shall be proceeded with in the Northwest territories before the court or judge named in such order, and thereupon the court or judge so named shall have jurisdiction to try such person.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 170, respecting juvenile delinquents.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Sir Eugene Fiset in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

Perhaps the minister will explain the circumstances under which this bill has been prepared. As I understand the matter, it has been very carefully gone over by a representative number of Canadians who are interested1 in questions respecting juvenile delinquents, and it Ijas met with the unanimous approval of various organizations and experts in that particular line of endeavour. If that be so, the minister might make an explanation that would expedite the passing of this proposed legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The bill arises entirely
out of recommendations made at a conference of the Canadian Council on Child Welfare, held in October last and attended by persons from all parts of Canada, representing the various agencies connected with the enforce-

Juvenile Delinquents
ment of the Juvenile Delinquents Act throughout the Dominion. The conclusions of the conference were the subject of a report to the department, and this bill embodies the suggestions made by the conference after a full discussion by judges, men at the head of this organization and officials of the Department of Justice. It is the old act with certain changes and improvements, all made with a view to facilitating the working of the Juvenile Delinquents Act.

Section agreed to.
On Section 2-Definitions.

If this legislation is to be
put into force, and each province is to have the right to change the age, will it not interfere greatly with the uniformity of the law? Why should one province declare that a juvenile delinquent may be eighteen years of age, while another declares that the age shall be sixteen?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no change as
to that. That was the old act. A mistake was made in the revision of the statutes, and the change which appears to be made now is simply for the purpose of restoring in that respect what was in the old act. It has always been so.

That is to say, under the
law as it is now each province may declare who is and who is not a juvenile delinquent according to age?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

This is the explanatory note in connection with section 2:
Under the 1908 act the age is sixteen years. The two provisos are to enable the governor in .council to provide by proclamation that the age may be raised to eighteen years in any particular province which desires it, and that such proclamation may have reference to boys or girls only, or to both.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the 1908 act the age is sixteen years. By chapter 37, section 1, of the statutes of 1921, that provision was repealed, and it was provided that "child" means a boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of eighteen years. But it was provided that the amendment should come into operation only in such province or provinces as the governor in council might from time to time by proclamation prescribe. The age is sixteen but, as my hon. friend says, it may be changed to eighteen when a province desires the change to be made.
Does this not seem anomalous?

Not in any sense to interrupt the explanation of the minister, I think the hon. member for Cartier will find the explanation in subsection (2) of section 3 of the act, which reads:
Where a child is adjudged to have committed a delinquency he shall be dealt with, not as an offender, but as one in a condition of delinquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision.
It was thought desirable by some of the provincial authorities to exercise help and guidance and proper supervision over some children who were older than sixteen years. Hence, sixteen being the standard, it is provided that by proclamation the governor in council may continue those provisions to children of the age of eighteen. That is, I think, the governing section of the whole of this legislation, namely, that a child is in a state of delinquency and is not an offender, but requires help and guidance and proper supervision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As a matter of fact, only in British Columbia was such a proclamation made raising the age to eighteen. In all the rest of Canada it is sixteen.

That is to say, in British Columbia they have only as much intelligence at eighteen as in the other provinces they have at sixteen. I should like to hear from the hon. member for Vancouver Centre in regard to that,

Paragraph (g) reads:
"Juvenile delinquent" means any child who violates any provision of the criminal code or of any Dominion or provincial statute, or of any by-law or ordinance of any municipality.
Is that not pretty broad?
It has always been that way.

Municipalities have many by-laws that are more or less trifling, and it is pretty hard to make a delinquent of a child who violates them. For example, there are by-laws that provide that you shall not scatter paper in the park or spit on the sidewalk. Surely you are not going to make a delinquent of a child who violates such by-laws as those.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Such a child would be treated with benevolence and rare. If it were an ordinary provision in. the criminal code, my hon. friend would certainly be right, but I would call his attention to the fact that the
Juvenile Delinquents

old act contains the same provisions; the only change is the striking out of certain words, namely:
For which violation punishment by fine or *imprisonment may be awarded.
The part which reads-
"Juvenile delinquent" means any child who violates any provision of the criminal code or of any Dominion or provincial statute, or of any by-law or ordinance of any municipality.
-was in the old act.
"For which violation punishment toy fine or imprisonment may be awarded."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those are the words that are asked to be struck out. I would hesitate to change the bill, because it was carefully considered and discussed by those most qualified to deal with it.
Does the minister mean then that imprisonment is abolished as regards a juvenile delinquent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that in the subsequent provisions of the bill the ordinary' imprisonment is abolished. But paragraph (g) is only a definition of what a juvenile delinquent is.

I should like to revert for a. moment to paragraph (g) of section 2, which refers to a child who is liable to be committed under the ordinance of any municipality. Suppose a child is haled into court for riding a bicycle on a sidewalk, which is a very common practice; would that constitute delinquency under this statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the leader of the
opposition said a few moments ago in reply to my hon. friend from Cartier, I think that the other provisions of the bill will help to a full understanding of the meaning and intent of the act. For instance, under section 3, where a child is adjudged to have committed a delinquency, he is to be dealt with, not as an offender, but as one in a condition of delinquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision. It is not for the purpose of punishment so much as for the purpose of helping the boy or the girl in question. The fact that violations of municipal by-laws are included among the offences which may constitute a child a delinquent is really not so serious because, after all, the purpose is simply to provide help and guidance and proper supervision.
And warning sometimes.

The hon. member for
Saskatoon has asked a question that some of my friends here were asking a few moments ago, and I have had some little discussion with those interested. There is no change in the section from what it was before. The child who rode a bicycle on the sidewalk would not be charged as an offender, but merely as a delinquent if thought desirable. If it were not for the provisions of this act he would be charged as an offender. That is the real distinction, and the whole purpose of the bill is that instead of the punishment that would be meted out to an offender, help and guidance and proper supervision shall be given and the child treated as a delinquent, not as an offender.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is based on kindness
rather than on anything else.

On kindness rather than
on punishment.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Delinquency.
May we have an explanation of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I really cannot make it clearer than the wording of the section itself. This is the collective wisdom of those who are dealing with these matters. Perhaps this section is not altogether necessary, but it is more for the purpose of explaining the principle upon which this whole legislation is based.

I really think the minister ought to give us some better explanation than that. I have every sympathy with legislation of this kind, but it does seem to me that in all such acts the one object should be reformation, to reclaim those who have transgressed the laws of the country and put them in the way of making of themselves good and reputable citizens. Along with that it must be remembered that punishment is a means to an end1, and I am rather afraid that much of the legislation we pass here has not that object in view, but rather that punishment is really punishment, instead of reform.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
By the other provisions
of the act sufficient punishment is provided, but as my hon. friend says, reformation is the principle underlying this bill. It is very likely that this section is not necessary, but it is harmless, and I believe it embodies a meritorious doctrine.

Juvenile Delinquents

Many such sections as
these appear to be harmless when they are passed by the house, but when placed in the hands of the law officers of the country to administer they are found not to be harmless, but rather detrimental, in my opinion, to the growth and development of character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will perhaps surprise
my hon. friend if I tell him that his objection was mine when this bill was submitted to me by the officers of the department. I also thought that this section, although finely worded, was not necessary, but they said that it was harmless and they would hesitate to advise that it be struck out because it was recommended by the child welfare organizations after very long and serious consideration.
I would recommend to the minister that he have the courage of his convictions and strike it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am always willing to
take the advice of others. On this bill I would prefer, perhaps to take the advice of the different bodies that met here last fall. Perhaps my hon. friend does not believe in them, but I do. There are many other matters on which I should be very glad to take the advice of my hon. friend.

Does the minister say
that he takes their advice against his own convictions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Ah well, may be.
Section 3 agreed to.
Sections 4 and 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Powers of judge of juvenile court.
Is provision made in all places for a juvenile trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

What about those districts in
which great harm is done and where there is no juvenile court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The act does not apply. It applies only in provinces where they ask that a proclamation be issued to apply the act, and in cities where a by-law is passed to that effect, and where it is proved that the necesary facilities for the enforcement of the act are available.

But thiq act
arranges for special trials in all cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
The minister knows the great harm done by magistrates in country districts who impose sentences out of all proportion to the offences committed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know that- The idea is to extend the act as much as possible, but it does not apply where proper facilities are not provided.

This would not apply
in Ontario except to such cities as Toronto, Hamilton and London?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot say from
memory all the places where it applies, but I know only last week we issued a proclamation applying it in the city of Oshawa.
It would not apply in the rural districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Section agreed to.
Sections 7 and 8 agreed to.
On section 9-Exceptional procedure when offence is indictable.
Have any representations been made to the Minister of Justice as to the advisability of changing this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I know there have
been complaints that too much responsibility is imposed upon juvenile courts. This section applies to indictable offences committed by juveniles who are apparently over the age of fourteen years. It is to be noted that discretion is given to the magistrate or to the juvenile court judge to order that the child be proceeded against by indictment. That is in the absolute discretion of the juvenile court. The section proceeds:
-but such course shall in no case be followed unless the court is of the opinion that the good of tlie child and the interest of the community demand it.
So that the juvenile court has the exclusive jurisdiction as to whether it shall try the offender or whether there shall be an indictment. In practice it is found that the juvenile court judge is more or less inclined to be very lenient with children who appear before him or her-in some places of course we have women juvenile court judges. Very serious offences are committed by boys who are almost men, and it is the gravamen of the complaints I 'have heard that in many cases these boys are not punished as they should be owing to the system in vogue in juvenile courts. I suggest there is some-
Juvenile Delinquents

thing worth considering in these complaints, and that there should be a change made in the section by adding these words:
-or on the application of the attorney general of the province where the offence is committed.
In such a case where the attorney general thought it advisable he would simply make application to the judge, and the judge would be bound to commit that child by way of indictment. The present practice does not work out very well, inasmuch as it is more or less an encouragement to the young hoodlums I am referring to to commit serious offences when they know they will not be adequately punished.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As my hon. friend will
notice, this is not a new section. The principle upon which the act is based is that even when children break the law they are still children and should be treated as such rather than as adult offenders. I would hesitate to accept the change mentioned by my hon. friend to take away discretion from the judge of the juvenile court, who is well acquainted with the conditions of the community, and to give that discretion to the attorney general. It is evident that the latter could not devote the same personal attention and personal oare to the conditions under which the offence may have been committed and in which the child finds himself as could the judge, or even the committee dealing with the question of children in that community. I believe the act has always worked well so far as this section is concerned, and that we should retain it.

I am rather inclined to
believe that there is something in the observations made by the hon. member for New Westminster. My attention was directed to a case in which a juvenile court judge was always inclined to err on the side of sentimental regard for the delinquent, with the result that certain rather grave offences were treated with a very great lack of seriousness. Would any injury be done to this statute if it provided:
Where the act complained of is, under the provisions of the criminal code or otherwise, an indictable offence, and the accused child is apparently or actually over the age of fourteen years,-
Fourteen years being the age at which intent may be presumed.
-the court or the attorney general of the province in which such court is situate-
Being the words used in section 7,
[DOT]-may, in its discretion, order the child to be proceeded against by indictment in the ordinary
[Mr. McQuarrie.l
courts in accordance with the provisions of the Criminal Code in that behalf; but such course shall in no case be followed unless the court or the attorney general is of the opinion that the good of the child and the interest of the community demand it.
There is no doubt that there must be a very sharp dividing line between the desire to bring about reform by kindly means and the regard for punishment. If an indictable offence has been committed-it must be indictable and the delinquent must be over fourteen years of age

there comes a time when it might well be that the sentiment of the presiding judge would lead to a course which would be injurious to the welfare of the country, and the attorney general, who after all has considerable responsibility under the criminal code, should be in a position to say, "It is quite clear that this is a case in which the ordinary course of justice should be followed, and the case heard as an ordinary charge against the provisions of the code". I do not think any injury can ensue from this, and it is just possihle that an untrained legal mind might realize that after all there was the principal officer of the crown to whom an appeal might be made in that regard. It is worth considering. My hon. friend from New Westminster has mentioned the matter, and the minister no doubt sees that there might be a case where it would be desirable to take this view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If our minds -are centred on punishment probably my hon. friend is right; his view is no doubt sound if we are thinking of punishment rather than of reform and improvement. I think however that the judge of the juvenile court is better situated to know whether it is more in the interests of the child and even of society that a boy should not be sent to an ordinary prison. I really cannot see that it would be in any way advisable to change the law.

I voice my personal
opinion when I say that extreme penalties, especially prison sentences, should be our last resort. When you imprison people a stigma follows them to the grave; that stigma falls also upon the wife of a -man as well as upon his children. To put a boy of fourteen or fifteen, or even sixteen or seventeen in a gaol for any offence without taking into consideration his education, his environment, his training or his parents is, I think, a very great mistake. We wish in this country to bring up respectable citizens, and I have always been opposed to gaol sentences except as extreme

Juvenile Delinquents
penalties. The object of all punishment is reform, and especially is this true when you are dealing with children who have not had the advantage of proper home influence, training and environment and whose mistakes or crimes, if you will, are committed in ignorance. I am very much opposed to taking the authority away from the local body and placing it in the hands of the attorney general.

Section agreed to.
Sections 10 and 11 agreed to.
On section 12-Names not to be published or identity of child indicated.
Does this include the publication of pictures? This has got to be a serious matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure it does.

This section speaks of a delinquency committed by a child. Under section 2 "child" means any boy or girl under the age of sixteen years. Now in section 9 we are providing that any child over the age of fourteen may be proceeded against by indictment in the ordinary course. Surely that is not consistent; if he is under sixteen he is a child and should not be so dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 9 deals with cases in which the child may be proceeded against under the provisions of the criminal code, in the discretion of the judge.
Nevertheless he is still a child.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but in that case it is in the discretion of the judge.
Does not the bon. gentleman know that a child of fourteen can be hanged for murder?
You have defined "child" as a person under sixteen; surely you will not proceed against a child by indictment.
A child can commit an offence.

The hon. gentleman has overlooked one fact. The criminal code provides that at the age of fourteen certain obligations rest upon every person, male or female, and section 9 of this act declares that the provisions of the criminal code may, if the judge so determines, become operative against that person if he or she is over fourteen. This
act provides that up to the age of sixteen the child shall be regarded as a delinquent. There is no inconsistency; section 9 relates to the criminal code, which provides that every person, male or female, becomes responsible in the eyes of the law at the age of fourteen.

Section agreed to.
Sections 13 to 15 inclusive agreed to.
On section 16-Court may adjourn or postpone hearing.
Just as a matter of information I should like to ask the Minister of Justice why all these sections which are not changed are reenacted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is a revision and consolidation of the act.

Section agreed to.
On section 17-Proceedings may be informal.

speechtext: I may say that the convention made a recommendation which went much further than this; they recommended that we should provide that any warrant or process issued by the juvenile court should run through all parts of the Dominion. In the department we thought it better to retain the limitation contained in the criminal code and to require that a warrant be endorsed by a judge in the district in which the arrest is to be made. I think there can be no objection to this section in its present form.

The same rule applies
under the criminal code.

Under this provision it would be possible to impose., a penalty upon

the parents of a child without their having an opportunity to be heard. I think this question should be carefully considered by the law officers of the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must confess that I was awaiting the reaction of the committee to this section. Personally I think it goes rather far, and if it were not for the fact that it was so strongly recommended by this convention I would hesitate to support it. I am quite willing to let this section stand.
The principle is ail right.

Without having a chance to be heard.

speechtext: I do not think parliament usually goes quite so far, I am quite willing to let this section stand for further consideration, and we may be able to suggest changes which will make it less objectionable.
